To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
effect-size measures can be expressed as correlations and can be calculated from t, and that the alerting correlation is useful for describing effect sizes in the presence of contrasts.

(a) effect sizes can be estimated from contrasts, (b) effect-size indices from contrasts are members of the correlation family, (c) effect-size correlations can be used to summarize data in a way that is both informative and interpretable, and (d) the alerting correlation and BESD correlation are especially useful in summarizing contrasts.

the alerting correlation is the correlation between two groups' means, the contrast correlation is the Pearson correlation between the two groups' scores, the effect-size index g is the correlation between the two group means and the difference between the two group's means, and the BSE index is the correlation between a group's score and the difference between that group's mean and a comparison group's mean.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods of effect-size estimation that are useful for answering focused questions about data.
the question of how best to present effect-size measures in the context of contrasts.

the development of effect-size indices that can be used to answer focused research questions, and with the development of a family of effect-size correlations that can be used with data from more complex research designs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
effect sizes can be estimated by means of contrasts and/or correlations, depending on the research question and on the nature of the data.

the alerting correlation is the best choice for reporting the effect-size correlation in the case of more than two groups; the contrast correlation is the best for reporting the contrast correlation; the BESD correlation is the best when a simple statement of effect size (e.g., the probability of success or failure) is desired; and the effect-size correlation is the best to use for meta-analytic purposes.
the effect-size correlation is the most useful of the four, but that the alerting and contrast correlations have their own advantages, especially in the context of a meta-analysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
contrasts are more informative than correlations, and correlations are more generalizable.
the correlational approach can be used to estimate effect size for all types of contrasts, and that contrasts and correlations can be used to ask focused and informative questions of data.
the g family and the r family of effect-size indices are both useful, but that the r family is the most flexible and interpretable.
The main takeaway from our work is that

effect-size measures are useful in the context of contrasts and that contrasts can be used to obtain useful effect-size measures in situations where contrasts are used to answer focused questions of data.
the alerting correlation can be calculated from any effect-size index and is a useful way of presenting results.
the effect-size indices are not interchangeable, even though they are all based on the same underlying data.
